5　The Marketplace and the Shop
1636年，葡萄牙耶稣会士曾德昭（Alvaro Semedo，约1585—1658）在中国传教二十余年之后，启程返回欧洲。面对故国读者，曾德昭描述了遥远的明中国药材供应之丰饶：“草药、根茎、果实、种子等等”。

In 1636, the Portuguese Jesuit Alvaro Semedo (c. 1585–1658) set sail back for Europe after serving as part of a mission to China for more than two decades. To the home audience, Semedo described the abundant supply of medicinal “herbs, roots, fruits, seeds, etc.” in distant Ming China:
“但诸般之中，医者所备尤足；因为他们从不开具处方，而是亲自把药交给所诊治的病人，且一切都在同一次出诊中完成。因此医者身后总跟着一名童子，背着一具五屉药箱，每屉又分为四十余小格，皆装满已研末、制好的药物。”

[B]ut of all others the Physicians are well provided; because they never write any receipt, but give the medicine themselves to the patient whom they visit, And all is done at the same visit, therefore the Physician hath alwayes following him a boy, carrying a Cabinet with five drawers, each of them being divided into more than fourty little squares; and all of them furnished with medicines ready ground and prepared.
曾德昭以毫不含糊的措辞确认，中国医者对治疗药库有着切身的掌控。那只精巧的药箱——便携、容量可观，又分隔为众多小抽屉——正是其主人宣称精通疗愈之术的象征。

In unequivocal terms, Semedo affirmed the Chinese physician’s intimate command over the therapeutic arsenal. The wonderful medicine cabinet—portable, capacious, and compartmentalized into numerous small drawers—epitomized its owner’s claim to expertise in the business of healing.
在曾德昭这番评论一个半世纪之后，负责长崎对外贸易的日本官员中川忠英在当地采访中国商人，编纂了一部图文并茂的清代中国日常生活志。据中川的受访者说：

One and a half centuries after Semedo’s comments, Nakagawa Tadahide, a Japanese official overseeing foreign trade in Nagasaki, interviewed Chinese merchants there and compiled an illustrated description of everyday life in Qing China. According to Nakagawa’s informants:
“绝无医者施药之事。无论病多重多急，医者都不自带药物。只有当（病人）从乡村僻远之地来请时，他们才带上药箱。这是因为乡间没有药铺，离市集又太远，于是医者便只好自带药箱前往。”

There is absolutely no such thing as medicines dispensed from the physician. No matter how grave and acute the illness is, physicians do not bring their own medicines. They only take their medicine cabinet when invitations [from the patient] come from rural and remote places. This is because there is no pharmacy in rural areas, and the distance is too far from a mar- ketplace, so that it becomes the case that physicians would bring their medicine cabinet with them.
商人们的回答描绘了这样一个世界：在能够便利通往市场的城市社区中，医者只开方而不施药、药师则照方抓药并配制成药，这种分工已成常态。于是，医者不得不自带药物的那些地方，便被界定为“僻远”与“乡野”。在清代文化中，界定一个地方处于中心还是边缘的，是商业交换的密集程度，而非地方官的官方品级。能否获得药物，成了能否获得资本的代名词。

The merchants’ answers described a world in which the division of labor between physicians, who prescribed without dispensing medicine, and pharmacists, who filled the formers’ prescriptions and dispensed compound drugs, was normalized in urban communities with good access to a marketplace. The places where physicians had to bring their own medicines then came to be defined as “remote” and “rural.” It was the intensity of commercial exchange, not the official ranking of the local administrator, that defined a place’s centrality or marginality in Qing culture. Access to pharmaceuticals became synonymous with access to capital.
关于帝制中国药业的历史，已有相当成熟的学术研究。多数学者同意，在十六至十八世纪间，两大发展塑造了明清中国病人获取药物的方式。首先，万志英（Richard von Glahn）所称这一时期“市场经济的成熟”，催生了广泛的批发贸易网络，向零售商大宗供应药材。
药材贸易本质上是跨区域的，因为从截然不同的地理区域采集的药材必须组合起来，才能配齐一座药房。结果，专营药材贸易的市镇成为重要的交换节点，在全国范围内为关键商品定价。
其次，研究十九世纪的史家常常注意到，城市成药铺日益显赫。这些店铺中最成功的企业家能够把品牌产品行销全国，积累惊人财富，并顺利地转化为地方乃至更大的影响力。

A well-established literature has examined the history of pharmaceutical enterprises in premodern China. Most scholars agree that between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, two major developments shaped the ways in which patients in Ming-Qing China acquired their remedies. First, what Richard von Glahn has called the “maturation of the market economy” during this period gave rise to an extensive network of wholesale trade that supplied materia medica in bulk to retailers.

This pharmaceutical trade was interregional by nature, for medicinal ingredients harvested from very different geographical regions must be combined to furnish a complete pharmacy. As a result, market towns (
shizhen
) specializing in pharmaceutical trade became important nodes of exchange, setting the price for key commodities on a national scale.

Second, historians of the nineteenth century frequently noted the rising prominence of urban dispensaries of compound medicine. The most successful entrepreneurs of these shops were able to market their brand-name products nationwide, accumulating staggering wealth that translated well into local influence and beyond.

药材贸易——无论批发还是零售——的增长，在多大程度上塑造了人们相对于我们在第四章所考察的正统医学的知识主张？徐大椿对药师的厌恶又在多大程度上是合理的？总体而言，市场中的男女并未在过去的本草药典中留下自己的声音。毋宁说，从五世纪的陶弘景到十一世纪的苏颂，本草编纂者都警告读者提防贸易中的欺诳与作伪，并试图以药典强加清晰与秩序。对数千种药物的整齐呈现，使人难以看出：药物的生产与配给，终究依赖于那些始终最关心自家生意兴隆者的劳动与创业。例如，我们从李时珍《本草纲目》中无法得知任何具体药物的价格，尽管作为仍在亲自配药的执业医者，他无疑对这类事情有切身了解。那些参与买卖数千种药材、货物来自中国不同地区和遥远异邦的众多中间人，我们几乎听不到他们的证词。可以说，本草药典的普遍性主张，恰恰建立在对波动的成本、价格、人力与逐利行为的刻意省略之上。

To what extent did the growth of the pharmaceutical trade, both wholesale and retail, shape claims to knowledge vis-à-vis the orthodox medicine we have examined in chapter 4? To what extent was Xu Dachun’s aversion to pharmacists justified? By and large, men and women of the marketplace did not find their voices recorded in past bencao pharmacopeias. If anything, compilers of bencao, ranging from Tao Hongjing of the fifth century to Su Song in the eleventh century, warned readers against the deception and fraud of the trade, and sought to impose clarity and order with the pharmacopeia. The uniform presentation of thousands of drugs made it difficult to see that, after all, the production and dispensing of medicine relied on the labor and entrepreneurship of those whose foremost concern had always been the wellness of their own businesses. We can gain no insight, for instance, about the prices of particular drugs from Li Shizhen’s
Bencao gangmu

, although, as a practicing physician still invested in compounding his own cures, he no doubt had intimate knowledge about these kinds of things. We hear hardly any testimony from the numerous middlemen who took part in buying and selling thousands of ingredients, sourced from different regions of China and distant foreign lands. One could argue that the claim to universality of the bencao pharmacopeias hinged precisely on the deliberate omission of fluctuating cost, price, human labor, and the pursuit of profit.

然而，若以为商业世界对精英医学的世界毫无影响，那也错了。在第二章中我们看到，药材的商品化回应了十六世纪的财政政策，并塑造了地方物产的记录方式。清朝的征服与长期战争，促成了原本彼此隔绝的生活的断裂与交融，从而产生了一种新的价值感，也塑造了商人与药师的自我形象。本章通过两个相互关联的个案，考察药材市场的文化意义。首先，我考察江西一个名为樟树的县级以下市镇的兴起（见地图0.1）：药材批发商在此聚集交易，各地货物被汇聚于此再行分销。其次，我重新审视文献记载丰富的同仁堂药铺史；该店约于1702年（康熙四十一年）在北京开业。我的论点是，像同仁堂这样的都会药铺，只有在晚明形成一体化批发市场之后才可能存在并运作。这些店铺不仅接管了国家收集、分配药材的职能，还在成药店售方面胜过个体医者经营的生意。市场与药铺都极为成功地表达并把自己的价值观注入清代主流文化。

Yet it would be wrong to assume that the world of commerce made no difference to the world of elite medicine. In chapter 2, we saw that the commodification of materia medica responded to fiscal policy in sixteenth century and shaped the documentation of local products. The Qing conquest and prolonged warfare facilitated the disruption and mingling of formerly separate lives, thereby generating a new sense of value that also shaped the self-image of traders and pharmacists. This chapter examines the
cultural

significance of the medicinal marketplace through two interconnected case studies. First, I examine the rise of a sub-county-level market town named Zhangshu, located in the Jiangxi Province (see map 0.1), where wholesale traders of materia medica gathered and traded, and supplies from all over the country were pulled together for redistribution. Second, I revisit the well-documented history of the pharmacy Tongrentang (Hall of Common Humanity), which opened for business in Beijing circa 1702 (Kangxi 41). My argument is that metropolitan pharmacies like Tongrentang could only exist and function after an integrated wholesale market came into existence in the late Ming. The shops not only took over the State’s role of collecting and redistributing materia medica, but also out-competed the businesses run by individual physicians in dispensing compound medicines. Both the marketplace and the pharmacy shop were highly successful in articulating and injecting their values to mainstream Qing culture.
宋明医药市场中的分工
Division of Labor in the Song-Ming Medical Marketplace
唐宋时期，医者本质上就是自配药物的店主。唐本草完整保留了陶弘景早先关于炮制的说明，并指导医者如何把既有方剂制成丸、散、膏、酒等剂型。诗人张籍（约766—830）困居唐都长安，抱怨被“药铺医人”多收了钱。
在长安划定设市的坊区里，人们认为医者容易沾染贪婪与欺诳，而这两者足以害德。被贬的官员柳宗元（773—819）在流放中撰文纪念一位奇人宋清；宋清在长安西市做买卖，向工匠型医者（yigong）供应生药。与其他商人不同，宋清从不向贫穷的欠债人追讨；最终，他得到的回报是丰厚的感激。在这篇名文末尾，柳宗元慨叹：在“市道”当令的时代，宋清之德何其稀少，即便官场亦然。

In Tang-Song times, physicians were essentially shop owners who compounded their own remedies. The Tang pharmacopeia preserved in full Tao Hongjing’s earlier instructions on pharmaceutical processing and instructed physicians on how to prepare an existing formula into dosage forms, such as pills, powders, ointments, and tinctures. Languishing in the Tang capital city Chang’an, the poet Zhang Ji (c. 766–830) complained about being overcharged by “physicians of the pharmacies” (
yaopu yiren

In the designated neighborhoods of Chang’an where markets were held, physicians were perceived as liable to the greed and deception that killed virtue. In his exile, the banished official Liu Zongyuan (773–819) wrote an essay commemorating an extraordinary man named Song Qing, who traded in the west market of Chang’an and supplied raw medicine to artisanal physicians (
yigong

). Unlike other merchants, Song never pursued his debtors who were poor; in the end, he was repaid handsomely with their gratitude. At the end of this celebrated essay, Liu lamented the rarity of Song Qing’s virtue in an age where the “Way of the Marketplace” (
shi dao
) reigned supreme, even in officialdom.

北宋的药材市场进一步多样化，其时城市已不再受严格分隔居住区与商业区的制度约束。

在全盛时期，北宋都城开封各坊拥有十余家医铺（yipu）。宋政府积极提倡医学，为许多精英医者授以官衔；他们开铺时自豪地张挂自己的头衔与专长，从儿科到产科不一而足。其中一家“赵太丞家”，被绘入《清明上河图》——北宋宫廷所创作、或许最负盛名的城市生活长卷。画家描绘赵姓医者在临街铺面中诊治一名小病人，铺前多处招牌宣传他的成药（见图5.1）。另一些店家则设计出抢眼的商标，如“银孩儿”“杜金钩”“任大鞋”“丑婆婆药铺”。
医学的商业性同样在南宋都城临安（后来的杭州）城市风貌记载中得到自豪的呈现，那里的医铺继续夸耀官方声望（“班防御家”）。
可以想见那些熙攘的街景，执业医者的店铺在其中赫然在目。

The medicinal marketplace in the Northern Song further diversified at a time when cities were no longer bound by strict rules separating residential and commercial quarters.
At the height of its prosperity, the Northern Song capital Kaifeng boasted over a dozen medical shops (
yipu

) in various neighborhoods of the city. The Song government’s active promotion of medical learning gave official ranks to many elite physicians who opened shops proudly displaying their titles and specialties ranging from pediatrics to obstetrics. One such shop, “medical officer Zhao’s home” (
Zhao taicheng jia
) was depicted in
Qingming shanghe tu (Along the River during the Qingming Festival

), arguably the most celebrated scroll painting of urban life created at the Song court. The artist depicted the physician Zhao treating a young patient in his shop opening onto the busy street, with multiple signs on display advertising his compound medicines (see figure 5.1). Others devised eye-catching trademarks such as “Silver Baby,” “Dr. Du the Golden Hook,” “Dr. Ren the Big Shoe,” or “Ugly Granny’s Medical Shop.”

The commercial nature of medicine was likewise proudly celebrated in documentations of the urban scene in the Southern Song capital Lin’an (later Hangzhou), where medical shops continued to boast official prestige (“Home of Defense General Ban”).
One could imagine the bustling street scenes, in which practicing physicians’ shops were an commanding presence.

史家通常引用一则十三世纪的轶事，作为中国出现综合性药铺的最早证据，那里作坊（zuofang）的生产空间与零售店面融为一体。然而细究之下，作者周密（1232—1298）实际上描述的是售卖“生药饮片”与“熟药圆散”的小贩，同时还卖蒸饼、烤肉、蜜饯枣、金橘。周密注意到，临安的生意人变得如此“骄惰”，凡事不肯从头制作，而是从“作坊”购买这些半加工产品。
这则轶事反映了宋代城市文化中制作工艺的精巧，但当时的预设仍然是：药铺主人应当自备药物。
Historians usually cite an anecdote dated to the thirteenth century as the earliest evidence for the emergence of general pharmacies in China, where the manufacturing space of a workshop (
zuofang
) was melded with the retail shop. Upon closer scrutiny, however, the author, Zhou Mi (1232–98), was in fact describing peddlers selling “raw medicine cut in pieces for decoction” (
shengyao yinpian
) and “cooked medicine in pills and powders” (
shuyao wansan

), along with steamed buns, roasted meats, preserved candy jujubes, and kumquat tangerines. Zhou noted that businesses of Lin’an became so “proud and idle” that they would not make everything from scratch but would purchase these half-processed products from “workshops” instead.
The anecdote reflected the sophistication of manufacturing processes in Song urban culture, and yet the assumption remained that medical shop owners should prepare their own remedies.

宋代的医者在经营管理店铺的同时，也认识到他们的多数常用药材来自遥远地区。在官方地理文献对土贡药材的统一标名之下，一种共识逐渐形成：最珍贵的药材来自王朝的西部与南部边疆。总体而言，宋代国家通过土贡获取某些地方物产的能力，可能因其疆域缩小而受限；因此，国家也积极参与药材贸易。本质上，中原药铺的大宗药材中，有不成比例的大份额来自四川（与青藏高原接壤）以及“广”的亚热带生境（“广”为广南的简称，后来分为广西、广东两省）。药材产地与精英医学实践的中心并不重合：十世纪晚期的一位作者记录了一句谚语，把最好的药归给四川，而只有都城长安才能找到最好的医者。
一个由（四）川与广（南）合成的简称“川广”，被评论者用来称赞一所由政府赞助、汇聚天下万物的慈善药局。
旅行者记录了他们对成都定期举行的“药市”的观察；成都是四川的主要行政中心。
从成都再往北，彰明县在宋代以大规模生产热性附子闻名（地图0.2）。在全盛时期，彰明每年向东输送十六万余磅附子，最好的一批总是送往“贵人”之手。
在临安这样的城市中心，定期的药市成为著名的茧桥集市的一部分；城中以白菊闻名，种植者便在菊花收获季节来此交易。
为获取最佳药材而采取的具体办法，塑造了每个城市社区的地方文化。

While managing and running their shops, Song physicians recognized the fact that most of their common ingredients had origins in distant regions. Beneath the uniform designation of tribute medicine in official geographical sources, a consensus emerged that the most precious medicinal ingredients came from the western and southern frontiers of the dynasty. Overall, the Song state’s access to certain local products through tribute was probably hampered by its reduced territorial extent and, as a result, the State actively took part in the pharmaceutical trade. In essence, the pharmacies of central China drew a disproportionate share of their major ingredients from the regions of Sichuan (bordering the Tibetan Plateau) and the subtropical habitat of Guang (a short form for Guangnan, later split into the provinces of Guangxi and Guangdong). The source of medicines and the center for elite medical practice did not overlap: a late tenth-century author recorded a proverb that delegated Sichuan as the home for the best medicines, whereas only in the capital city of Chang’an could one find the best physicians.

A shorthand term, Chuan-Guang, consisting of (Si)chuan and Guang(nan), was used by commentators in praise of a government-sponsored charitable pharmacy assembling every imaginable product of the world.
Travelers recorded their observations of “medicinal market fairs” (
yaoshi
) regularly held in Chengdu, the major administrative center of Sichuan.
Further north from Chengdu, the district of Zhangming became known for large-scale production of the hot-natured aconite root (
fuzi
) in Song times (map 0.2). At its height, Zhangming sent over 160,000 pounds of aconite roots eastward every year, and the best batch always went to “noble people” (
guiren
In urban centers such as Lin’an, regular medicinal fairs were held as a part of the famed Cocoon Bridge (
Jianqiao
) fair, where cultivators of the city’s well-known variety of white chrysanthemum traded during its harvest season.
Specific solutions for sourcing the best pharmaceutical ingredients shaped the local culture of each urban community.

宋代中国的商业文化由此扩展了执业医者的药物储备。医者视执业地点，可能选择依靠多种供应渠道的组合：药市（若有可能）；从山林采药的本地采集者；以及自家药园，用于有限数量的家种药用植物。
药学在医学实践中的核心地位，因所谓“药室”（yaoshi）的兴起而凸显；这一术语源自道教炼丹文献，后来成为私家医业的场所通称。从十三至十五世纪，许多医者请名士撰写纪念文章，借机为店铺取一个好字号，往往沿循仁爱利他的儒学意涵。
药室的经营本质上成为一种家族事业，元与明初国家以世袭“医户”（yihu）的身份予以承认。药室的世袭品牌将为清代都会药铺提供重要先例，尽管我们将会看到，店主医学专长的核心地位在后来的时代逐渐淡出焦点。

Commercial culture in Song China thus extended the pharmaceutical repertoire of practicing physicians. Depending on one’s location of practice, a physician might choose to rely on a combination of suppliers: market fairs (if possible); local collectors who picked herbs from mountains and forests; and one’s own medicinal garden, for a limited number of domesticated medicinal plants.
The centrality of pharmacy in medical practice was highlighted by the rise of the so-called pharmaceutical chambers (
yaoshi

), a term derived from Daoist alchemical treatises that came to be used as a common appellation for the space of proprietary medical practices. From the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, many physicians solicited commemorative essays from famous literati and used the opportunity to get a good brand name for their shop, often along the Confucian lines of benevolence and altruism.
The maintenance of a pharmaceutical chamber became essentially a family business as recognized by the Yuan and early Ming state in the status of hereditary “medical households” (
yihu

). The hereditary branding of pharmaceutical chambers would provide an important precedent for Qing metropolitan pharmacies, although as we shall see the centrality of the owner’s medical expertise would drift out of focus in later times.
十五世纪初的一份稀见记载，让我们得以一窥某位医者经营药室的日常管理。文中所描绘的职业生活远非光鲜，而与处理体面、礼节以及物料开支带来的成本等世俗关切密切相关：

An unusual account in an early fifteenth-century source gives us a rare peek into the day-to-day management of a physician-run pharmaceutical chamber. The professional life depicted in this text was far from glamorous and had everything to do with the mundane concern of managing propriety, courtesy, and cost incurred by material expenses:
早起晏眠，不可片时离店中。凡有抱病者至，必亲自诊视，用心发药，莫仍前只靠郎中，惟务安闲。
Rise early and retire late, do not leave your shop even for a moment. When a patient comes, make a careful diagnosis, and dispense the drugs. Never ever entrust it to your assistant.
……照彼中乡原立价，一则有益于己，二则同道不怪。仍可饶药，不可减价。

. . . Price [your remedies] according to local custom; this is good for you and also will not annoy your fellow practitioners. You might want to occasionally give away drugs for free, but do not lower the price.

……行医及开首发药，当根据经方写出药贴，不可杜撰药名，胡写秘方，受人驳问。

. . . When dispensing a remedy for the first time, write out the prescription according to the Classical formula. Do not invent fake drug names or write nonsense secret recipes, for people will later scold you on that.
郎中磨作，量其所入，可用几人。莫言人多好看，工价虽廉，食用甚贵。

As for assistants and compounding laborers, only hire a couple of them, depending on your income. Don’t say that it makes your shop look good with more helping hands. Although the labor is cheap, lodging and food are very expensive.
及有行院干谒，送至茶笔扇帕之类，初焉便不可接，当赠汤药一二帖，连物回还。
If you receive gifts from solicitous courtesans or theatre troupes, such as tea, fans and handkerchiefs . . . never accept them. Return them with a couple packs of medicine for decoction.
这段文字表明，医者的职业权威与社会地位，在许多方面取决于对店铺的有效经营与实际配药。可以说，当时并不认为医者的学术品质与创业品质彼此冲突。我们将看到，这种预设如何在明末开始动摇。

The text indicates the extent to which a physician’s professional authority and social standing depended, in many ways, on the effective management of a shop and the dispensing of actual remedies. The scientific and entrepreneurial qualities of a medical practitioner, so to speak, were not seen as being in conflict with each other. We shall see how such assumptions faltered toward the end of the Ming dynasty.
晚明道地性的重构
Reconfiguring Authenticity in the Late Ming
不断延伸的药材供应链，使许多人对市场的反复无常心生警惕。我们在第二章看到，地方志的编纂者甚至删去地方物产的记载，以免招来不必要的关注。十六世纪初的一部方志抱怨财富正从较贫之地流向富处：“物丰于所聚，利竭于所产。”
织者得不到足够的衣料；采药者不用药来治病。因此，晚明许多财政改革活动家发现自己主张更多地、而非更少地依赖商业利益，这不能不说具有讽刺意味。到了晚明，后者的术语与价值观终于渗透到当时的普遍文化之中。

Ever-extending supply chains of pharmacy made many wary of the capriciousness of the marketplace. We saw in chapter 2 how editors of local gazetteers went so far as to delete records of local products so as to avoid unwanted attention. An early sixteenth-century gazetteer complained that wealth was being extracted from poorer places in favor of the rich: “Abundance comes from the assembly of things; profit stays meager where they are produced.”

The weavers could not get adequate clothing; those who picked medicinal herbs did not use them to cure their diseases. It was thus not without irony that many activists for fiscal reform in late Ming found themselves advocating for more, not less, dependency on mercantile interests. In late Ming times, the latter’s terminology and values did eventually seep through the general culture of the day.

最显著的话语转变之一，在于药材贸易与一种新的地方本真性观念之间的特定关联，这一观念以“道地”一词表达。字面意为“道路与地方”，此词至迟在十三世纪已获得地方特定性——因而对本源的真实性——的含义。
随着土贡药材折银，商人从遍布全国的政府采购中大发其财，把药材供应到最能获利的地方。如果说土贡药材的货币化使药材脱离了传统产地，那么商业交换又把它重新地方化到新的地点，同时创造出关于同与异的新话语。据英文底本概述，1640年代的一部方志指出，药材贵在道地，否则无异于野草。
本真性的语言如今不再出自官方规定，而是出自商人的世界。

One of the most salient discursive shifts lies in the specific connection between the pharmaceutical trade and a new notion of place-based authenticity, articulated by the term
daodi
. Literally meaning “routes and places,” the term acquired the meaning of place-based specificity—and hence authenticity to one’s origins—no later than the thirteenth century.

Following the conversion of tribute medicine into silver, merchants made good fortunes from widespread governmental purchases all over the country, supplying materia medica to the places where the greatest profit could be made. If the monetization of tribute medicine delocalized a medicinal herb from its traditional origins, commercial exchange relocalized them to new places, thereby creating at the same time new discourses of sameness and difference. “Medicines gain their value from authentic sources (
daodi
),” noted a gazetteer in the 1640s, “or else they are mere weeds.”
The language of authenticity now came not from governmental stipulations but from the world of traders.

药材一体化长途贸易的兴起，悄然改变了药物消费者的态度与预设。剧作家汤显祖（1550—1616）也是江西人，他在名剧《牡丹亭》中使用了“道地药材”一词。在一封私人书信中，汤显祖解释自己绝不可能迁居北京，因为“道地精药多不至北”。
同样，1630年代，杭州本草学者卢之颐随意评论药材供应道：

The rise of integrated long-distance trade in materia medica quietly altered the attitudes and assumptions held by consumers of medicine. The playwright Tang Xianzu (1550–1616), also a native of Jiangxi, used the term “daodi materia medica” in his famous play
Peony Pavillon
. In a personal letter, Tang explained how he could not possibly relocate to Beijing, for “authentic and refined medicines mostly do not reach the North.”
Similarly, writing in the 1630s, the Hangzhou-based bencao scholar Lu Zhiyi casually commented on the supply of materia medica:
“药产古今不同。……古人用药，取之中原而有余。今多采之遐方远裔，其近产者绝不足用。”

The production of medicine is different in ancient and modern times. . . . Ancient people harvested from the Central Plains and got more than what they needed. Nowadays, most medicines are obtained from distant lands and faraway peoples (
xiafang yuanyi
), for products from nearby sources are by no means adequate.
对卢之颐这样老练的城市居民而言，药材的总体供应——而不只是珍贵昂贵的原料——如今都依赖远方长途贸易，这已是平淡无奇的事实。
To sophisticated urbanites like Lu Zhiyi, it was a banal fact that the
general
supply of medicines, not just precious or expensive ingredients, now depended on long-distance trade from faraway places.
精英顾客期望的提高，给医者维持所施药材质量的能力提出了新问题。徽州医者陈嘉谟在1565年刊行的本草入门书中引用一句俗谚，表达药师与医者之间的权力失衡：“卖药者两只眼，用药者一只眼，服药者全无眼。”
在晚明文学中，常常成为众矢之的的，是医者而非药师。一篇晚明短篇小说描写一位白手起家的医者如何得到一位慷慨商人的资助，获得开业资金与货源。那商人这样描述这门生意：

Rising expectations on the part of elite customers posed new questions for the physicians’ ability to maintain good quality for the material remedies they dispensed. In his bencao primer published in 1565, the Huizhou physician Chen Jiamo quoted a folk idiom to express this power imbalance between pharmacists and physicians: “The drug-seller has two eyes; the physician has only one eye; the patient has no eye at all.”

It was physicians, not pharmacists, who frequently became popular targets of ridicule in late Ming literature. A late Ming short story describes how a self-made physician received help from a generous trader for the start-up funds and supplies of his business. The trader describes that business as follows:
“别人家买药的，就要现钱才卖。只有行医开铺的，是长久主顾，但要药料，只上个账簿取去，或一季、或一月一算，总数还钱，叫做半赊半现。”

I only accept cash when other people buy medicine from me, except for physicians who practice in shops, who are my long-term customers. If they need anything, they just take it from me and leave a note on the account book. I collect money from them every season [three months] or every month according to the sums, and this is called half-loan-half-cash.
商人把话说得很明白：医者依赖他供应药室，而只有他有权追讨医者的欠款。我们或许记得，如第三章所论，万历朝（1573—1620）也正是缪希雍这类绝艺医者开始仅凭处方行医、“不带药囊”的时期。我们可以开始看到，商人与供应商——或许堪比早期近代欧洲的“药剂师”（apothecaries）行业——迁入疗愈领域，从而使他们有可能被视为药师。

In very clear terms, the trader laid bare the fact that physicians relied on him for supply of their pharmaceutical chambers, and that he alone had claim on the latter’s debt. We might recall, as I discussed in chapter 3, that the Wanli reign (1573–1620) was also when virtuoso physicians such as Miao Xiyong started to practice by prescription alone, “without carrying a bag of medicine.” We could start seeing the migration of traders and suppliers—perhaps comparable to the trade of “apothecaries” in early modern Europe—into the realm of healing, making it possible to see them as pharmacists.
晚明的城市景观画，如各种版本的所谓《苏州片》，也暗示了医学与市场之间那种难以确定的张力。

其中一幅绘制最精的长卷摹仿名画家仇英（约1494—1552）的风格，采用了许多十二世纪《清明上河图》的母题，包括医者那间位置显眼的店铺；画中可见他为孩童诊病、书写处方。与医者庄重的店面相对，一家供应“道地药材”的药铺被描绘在城市的另一街区。店中挤满等候的顾客，药铺伙计忙于切药、抓方。墙上挂着成串的新鲜与干燥药草以及葫芦容器，架柜上堆满各种药材。一只尾巴完整、四肢俱全的爬行动物固定在店堂天花板上。那动物大概是鼍的标本——一种原产于长江中下游水道的淡水小鳄。李时珍在《本草纲目》中指出，鼍皮在药铺中有用，因为药肆常悬挂鼍甲，称其“能辟蠹”。
通过描绘两个截然不同的疗愈空间，这类长卷提供了满足不同消费者需求的城市空间原型。
Urban landscape paintings of the late Ming, such as the many versions of the so-called Suzhou Scrolls (
Suzhou pian
), also suggested the indeterminate tension between medicine and the marketplace.

One of the most finely executed scrolls, in imitation of the style of the famous artist Qiu Ying (c. 1494– 1552), adopted many motifs from the twelfth-century Qingming Scrolls, including the physician’s prominently featured shop, in which he could be seen treating a child and writing prescriptions. In contrast to the dignified shop front of the physician, a pharmacy shop supplying “authentic materia medica” (
daodi yaocai

) was depicted in a different quarter of the city. Densely packed with waiting customers, the pharmacy clerks busily chopped herbs and filled the prescriptions. Strings of fresh and dried plants and calabash gourd containers hung on the wall, and shelves and cabinets overflowed with various materials. A reptilian animal with an intact tail and four limbs was fixed to the ceiling of the shop. The animal was probably a
tuo
specimen, a small, freshwater alliga- tor native to the middle and lower Yangzi waterways. In
Bencao gangmu
, Li Shizhen noted that the skin of the tuo was useful in pharmacies, for it was believed that the animal could “dispel moths and worms and prevent the
materia medica
from decay.”
By depicting two very different spaces of healing, scrolls such as this one offered prototypes of urban spaces that met the needs of different consumers.

On this expedition I will take the overland route by way of Henan-Shanxi-Hanzhou on the way out, and return on the water route by way of Xiajiang and Jingzhou. The round-trip will amount to seven or eight thousand

西门达、孟锐这样的个体商人，沿着繁荣的旅行指南与路程书记载的水陆路线，穿梭于明代的疆域。孟锐的行程，很可能就是晚明普通“川广”客商的典型（见下文地图5.1）。走艰辛的西行旱路，孟锐会在华东、华中买下纸张、蜡等制成品，再到川广出售。西行返程时，他会购买川广的道地物产，可能包括药材，运回家乡作为消费品出售。川广的新鲜物产价值高、又易腐坏，最宜先顺长江中下游而下，再沿大运河向北运回。
行商的辛劳，源于这样一种前景：只要积累足够的资本，有朝一日便可在好地方定居，开设自己的店铺。《金瓶梅》的故事表明，成功的商人把财富传给下一代，并不罕见。
编者说明：底本把返程称为“西行”，但本段前文已称去程西行，下文又描述沿长江顺流及运河北返；方向表述之间存在疑点，此处保留底本。

Individual dealers such as Ximen Da and Meng Rui crisscrossed Ming territory along the water and land routes that were documented in the thriving genre of travel guides and route books. Meng Rui’s itinerary may well have been typical for an average “Chuan-Guang” guest merchant in late Ming times (see map 5.1 below). By taking the onerous westbound route overland, Meng would have bought manufactured goods such as paper and wax in east and central China, and then sold them in Chuan-Guang. For the westbound return trip, he would have bought daodi products from Chuan-Guang, possibly including materia medica, and brought them to sell as consumer products back home. High in value and likely perishable, the fresh products of Chuan-Guang traveled best on boats first downstream on the mid- and lower Yangzi River, and then back north along the Grand Canal.
The toil of traveling merchants was motivated by the prospect that, with enough accumulated capital, they could one day settle down in a good location and establish their own shops. The story of
Jin ping mei
suggests that it was not uncommon for successful dealers to pass on their wealth to the next generation.

医者与药师角色的颠倒，在《金瓶梅》情节中也清晰可见。西门庆本人不通医理，却不止一次欺辱、嘲弄医者。第十七回，李瓶儿与西门庆疏远，改嫁一位普通医者蒋竹山。蒋竹山每为病人开一方药，只赚五分银子；李瓶儿却给他三百两银子，让他开一间大门面，备足川广药材。两回之后，怀恨在心的西门庆派人骚扰蒋竹山。他们殴打他，砸毁他的店铺，逼他离开李瓶儿；李瓶儿最终成为西门庆的第六房妾。蒋竹山失去了偶然得来的全部资本，只带着“药材、药碾、药筛、药箱”搬走。

The inversion of the roles of physician and pharmacist was also seen clearly in the plot of
Jin ping mei

. On more than one occasion, physicians become the targets of bullying and mockery by Ximen Qing, who is himself ignorant of medical theory. In chapter 17, Li Ping’er becomes estranged from Ximen and instead marries an ordinary physician named Jiang Zhushan. Whereas Jiang only earns about five cents of silver for each medication he prescribes to a patient, he receives three hundred liang of silver from Li to open a large shop front with an abundant supply of Chuan-Guang medicine. Two chapters later, a vengeful Ximen Qing sends his men to harass Jiang. They beat him, demolish his shop, and force him to leave Li Ping’er, who eventually becomes Ximen’s sixth concubine. Losing all the capital he had gained haphazardly, Jiang Zhushan moves out with only the “medicines, grinders, sieves, and medicine cabinets” to his name.

第五十四回，李瓶儿因与西门庆所生之子夭折，身体每况愈下。一位姓任的世医被请来诊治。任医官虽摆出博学医者的派头，西门庆却额外送上一两银子，催他快些。小说1613年版特别写到，西门庆打开任医官“药室”送来的药包，称赞任医官礼数周到，不但送来煎药的材料，还附上预先配好的丸药。
然而，在1640年代出现的同一小说另一版本中，任医官与西门庆相见的情节被大幅改写。任氏药室送药的详细描写不见了，讽刺转而集中于这位儒医（ruyi）对西门庆的谄媚交谈。
很可能到1630年代，从医者药室获取成药的细节，在精英读者眼中已经过时。对任医官医术的敬意退入背景，留下的只是财富与权力的丑恶面孔。
In chapter 54, Li Ping’er’s health has deteriorated due to the premature death of her son with Ximen Qing. A lineage physician (
shiyi

) surnamed Ren is summoned to treat her. Although Ren acts with the air of a learned physician, Ximen Qing makes him hasten his service with the additional tip of one ounce of silver. The 1613 edition of the novel highlights the moment when Ximen opens the medication package delivered from Ren’s “pharmaceutical chamber” and comments that Ren is courteous enough to send along not only the ingredients to make a decoction, but also compound pills he prepared in advance.

In a later edition of the same novel that appeared in the 1640s, however, the portrayal of Ren’s encounter with Ximen Qing was revised significantly. Gone was the detailed description of a delivery from Ren’s pharmaceutical chamber, and the satire focuses instead on the Confucian doctor’s (
ruyi
) obsequious conversations with Ximen Qing.

It may very well be that by the 1630s, the detail of getting compound medicine delivered from a physician’s medicine chamber already appeared out of fashion to elite readers. The trace of respect for physician Ren’s medical skill recedes into the background, and all that remains is the ugly face of wealth and power.
“药码头”的形成
The Making of a “Medicinal Wharf”

现在让我们转向另一则关于晚明药材商人的故事。它收于一部题为《杜骗新书》的劝诫故事集，初刊于1617年。主人公是一位名叫于定志的商人，来自西南的云南。于定志的生意之旅，始于在四川把一批干栀子卖了八十两银子。他随即用这笔现银买下几担当归与川芎——二者都是四川原产、常用于方剂的药材。于定志雇了几名脚夫挑担，又租船顺长江而下。然而他们的目的地并非人口稠密的下游江南，而是江西赣江边一个名为樟树的小市镇（见地图5.1）。运费为每担二两六钱。
Let us now turn to another story told about late Ming medicinal traders. It is included in a collection of cautionary tales titled
Dupian xinshu (The Book of Swindles

), first published in 1617. The main protagonist, a trader named Yu Dingzhi, hails from the southwestern province of Yunnan. Yu’s business trip starts with the sale of a batch of dried gardenia fruit (
zhizi
) for eighty liang of silver in Sichuan. He then uses the cash to buy several loads of angelica (
danggui
) and Sichuanese lovage (
chuanxiong

), both native plants of Sichuan frequently used in medical formulas. Yu hires a few laborers to carry the loads and rents a boat to sail downstream along the Yangzi River. Their destination, however, was not the densely settled area of Lower Yangzi, but a small market town called Zhangshu, located in the province of Jiangxi along the Gan River (see map 5.1). The shipping costs amount to two liang and six
qian
per load.
到了樟树，于定志住进一家由本地牙人（yaren）经营的客栈。牙人提出以每担十两买他的当归，川芎每担六两。于定志想等更好的价钱，拒绝了。日复一日，更多客商（keshang）带着更充足的川药来到樟树，买价越压越低。

In Zhangshu, Yu checks in to a lodge run by a local broker (
yaren
), who proposes to buy his angelica at ten liang per load, and lovage for six liang per load. Yu decides to wait for a better deal and declines the offer. Day after day, more guest merchants (
keshang
) arrive in Zhangshu with even more abundant supplies of Sichuanese drugs, and the buying-in price drops lower and lower.

最终，于定志被迫带着药材离开市镇，继续东行，最后在福建建宁府以每担三两七钱的惨淡价格把货卖出。

In the end, Yu is forced to leave the town with his herbs and head further east, eventually selling off his wares in the Jianning Prefecture, Fujian, at the dismal rate of three liang and seven qian per load.
故事的寓意是：明智的商人应警惕贪心过盛，盲目追求最高利润只会导致破财。

尽管人物与经历都是虚构的，故事却让我们真切感受到支配晚明药材批发贸易的地理逻辑与季节节律。于定志这样的个体商贩彼此竞争，把四川土产运往下游，他们的需求滋养了沿水路形成的脚夫与船运服务链。交易的频繁与密集，足以在樟树镇生成一个集中市场。与《金瓶梅》的故事不同，商人们并不进城与潜在买家讨价还价，而是聚集在一个镇上，由（政府合法发牌的）牙人招待各方生意伙伴，促成交易。市场对供求波动也足够敏感，片刻迟疑便可能造成重大损失。四川收获的季节节律，会立刻导致数千里外下游樟树的价格下跌。当于定志这样的人在樟树看不到获利空间时，便不得不额外费力前往远离主要商路的地方（例如福建腹地），按当地价格把货卖掉。
The moral of the story is that a wise merchant should be wary of excessive greed, and that the blind pursuit of the highest profit only results in financial ruin.

Although the characters and their adventures were fictional, the story nevertheless gives us a very real sense of the geographical logic and seasonal rhythms that dominated the wholesale trade of materia medica in late Ming China. Individual dealers such as Yu competed with one another to transport local Sichuan products downstream, and their demand nurtured a supply chain of laborers and shipping services along the waterways. The frequency and intensity of business transactions were enough to generate a centralized marketplace in the town of Zhangshu. Unlike the story of
Jin ping mei

, the dealers did not travel into cities to bargain with potential buyers, but instead assembled in one town, where brokers (legally licensed by the government) hosted all business partners to make deals. The marketplace was also sensitive enough to fluctuating supply and demand that a short moment of delay could result in major losses. The seasonal rhythms of harvest in Sichuan promptly resulted in the plunging prices at Zhangshu, thousands of miles away down the river. When someone like Yu saw no room for profit in Zhangshu, they would have to make the extra effort to travel to places further away from the main trade routes (for example, hinterland Fujian) and sell off their goods with the local prices there.

樟树在哪里？在明代中国的行政层级中，樟树是一个镇，隶属清江县知县管辖。清江县城同时也是临江府治所，城墙环绕；樟树则是没有城墙的市镇。二者分处赣江东西两岸，隔水相望，以渡船相连。镇名意为“樟树”，可能与当地樟树繁茂有关；另有一则传说，说一位古代武士曾追逐一头鹿，一箭射入老樟树，因而得名。浩浩赣江发源于南岭北麓，自那里北流，穿过江西，最后汇入长江。沿途小水道把赣江航线东连福建、西接湖广。在清江—樟树，赣江与袁水相汇；袁水可航，通往湖南腹地。自十三世纪以来，清江、樟树一带便与药材贸易相关，部分原因是附近阁皂山作为道教名山的声誉。
元灭宋后迁居樟树的士人侯逢丙，以开设慈善药局、免费施送良药闻名。然而，没有证据表明区域性药材贸易在十五世纪以前已集中于樟树。
Where is Zhangshu? In the administrative hierarchy of Ming China, Zhangshu was a town (
zhen

) that fell under the jurisdiction of the magistrate residing in Qingjiang (clear water) County. The walled city of Qingjiang, which also served as the administrative seat of the Linjiang Prefecture, and the unfortified town of Zhangshu were located respectively on the west and east bank of the Gan River, facing each other and connected by ferries. The town’s name, meaning “camphor trees,” may have been related to the abundance of such trees in the region, whereas a legend attributed it to an ancient warrior who once chased a deer and shot an arrow into an old camphor tree. The mighty Gan River originates from the northern ridge of the Nanling Mountains and flows north from there, cutting through the Jiangxi Province before finally joining the Yangzi River. Along the way, minor waterways connect the Gan route to Fujian in the east and Huguang in the west. At Qingjiang-Zhangshu, the Gan is joined by the Yuan River, a navigable waterway that leads to the hinterland of Hunan. Since the thirteenth century the region of Qingjiang and Zhangshu had been associated with the medicinal trade, owing in part to the fame of the nearby Gezao Mountain as a Daoist site.

Hou Fengbing, a literatus who moved to Zhangshu after the Mongol conquest, was known for his charitable pharmacy that distributed effective cures for free. Yet there is no evidence indicating that interregional trading of materia medica concentrated in Zhangshu prior to the fifteenth century.
当地人提出两种叙事，解释樟树何以崛起为跨区域贸易的中心市场。一种为本地士人所偏爱的说法，与明代藩王朱宸濠（卒于1521年）那场不幸的叛乱有关；朱宸濠的封地在江西省城。传说商人们为躲避这位藩王暴政所加的沉重税负，才从清江迁到对岸的樟树。
另一种说法把原因归于嘉靖朝（1522—1566）赣江突然改道。赣江不再在清江县城脚下与袁水相会，而是径直向北切流，在樟树镇门前与袁水相汇。于是，往来广东的船只日益停靠樟树镇，绕过了县城。
十六世纪中叶，当地人重修庙宇，并在镇前水滨修筑了壮观的堤岸。
到十六世纪末，樟树作为“药码头”的名声已牢固确立。
据英文底本概述，商人手册称此镇是天下药材会聚之地，南北商贾云集。
阅历广博的作者王士性（1547—1598）估计，这座“雄镇”中有逾万户人家，颇为繁盛。
当地人指出，樟树不仅交易药材，还交易木材、器具与衣物，然后销往东南各郡。
总之，一个昔日默默无闻的县级以下市镇，开始引起全国瞩目。

Locals suggested two narratives that explained Zhangshu’s rise into a central marketplace for interregional trade. One story, favored by local literati, had to do with the ill-fated rebellion of Zhu Chenhao (d. 1521), a Ming prince whose fiefdom was located at the provincial capital of Jiangxi. Legend had it that merchants relocated across the river from Qingjiang to Zhangshu in order to get away from the heavy tax imposed on them by the tyranny of the prince.

A second story attributed the cause to the Gan’s sudden change in course during the Jiajing reign (1522–66). Instead of meeting the Yuan right at the foot of the walled city of Qingjiang, the Gan now cut directly north and met the Yuan at the doorstep of Zhangshu. River traffic to and from Guangdong therefore increasingly docked at the town of Zhangshu, bypassing the county seat.
During the mid-sixteenth century, locals rebuilt temples and constructed impressive dykes that lined the town’s waterfront.
By the late sixteenth century, Zhangshu’s fame as a “medicinal wharf” (
yao matou
) had been firmly established.
Merchant handbooks referred to the town as the “meeting place of medicines from all country,” where “merchants from north and south” came together.
Wang Shixing (1547–98), a well-traveled author, estimated a total of over ten thousand households “thriving” in the “imposing town” (
xiongzhen
Locals noted that not only materia medica but also timber, utensils, and clothing were traded in Zhangshu and then sold “to the southeastern prefectures.”
In sum, a formerly obscure sub-county-level market town started to attract national attention.

晚明地方官对樟树的新财富反应复杂。与围绕地方土贡改革的广泛行动相似，清江精英憎恶北京派来为皇室采买的宦官使臣，视其扰乱地方秩序。
地方志还带着几分警惕，记载了十七世纪初起加于该镇的日益沉重的税负：先来自府，后来直接来自北京当局。
到1630、1640年代，明廷为筹措边防与平叛经费的绝望挣扎，导致对南方加征更严酷的附加税。地方知县认为，樟树的好运到头了。

Local administrators in the late Ming reacted to Zhangshu’s newfound fortune with mixed feelings. Similar to the widespread activism that had surrounded the reform of local tribute, the Qingjiang elite detested eunuch envoys sent from Beijing to purchase goods from the market town for the throne, seeing it as disruptive of local order.

The gazetteer also documented, with certain wariness, the increasing tax burden on the town beginning in the early seventeenth century, first from the prefecture, then directly from authorities in Beijing.

By the 1630s and 1640s, the Ming state’s desperate attempt to fund border defense and antirebellion campaigns resulted in even more punishing surtaxes on the south. The local magistrate thought that the good fortune of Zhangshu was over.
使地方政治更加复杂的，是外来商人的涌入：他们住在樟树，却为自身跨区域利益行事。用一位知县的话说，“客胜主”。

This episode indicated that the local community understood the logic of commerce very well, and that it took constant vigilance to keep the center of trade in their town.

The marketplace of Zhangshu offered Fang Yizhi an abundance of differences coded in regional origins (Huai versus Sichuan) and measured by sensual data (color, texture, shape). Here, Fang Yizhi simply recorded what he had learned without attempting to explain the varieties in terms of their cosmic natures. Fang was reticent about how this kind of knowledge could pave the way to a clearer understanding of the principle of things (

清廷对药材贸易的重商主义政策
Qing Mercantilist Policy toward Pharmaceutical Trade

清初征服后的最初数十年，不确定性笼罩一切：新王朝的满洲统治者要应对其治下广袤土地的制度与习俗。他们会延续晚明把多样税基货币化的推动，还是回归以实物征收地方土贡的旧原则？地方官能在多大程度上为本辖区争取减税？他们会鼓励跨区域与海外贸易吗？若鼓励，此类交易允许在何处进行，国家又从利润中抽取多少？一如文化领域，清代财政政策也花了一些时间，才重新配置国家与其税基的关系。药物物性问题再次显示了清廷治理的路径，因为充足的药材供应对国家生计始终至关重要。清代不同政府部门获取药物的方式，由此构成十八世纪药材贸易及其他商业事业持续发展的重要背景。

Uncertainty loomed large in the initial decades following the Qing conquest, as the Manchu rulers of the new dynasty reckoned with the institutions and customs of the vast land they now governed. Would they continue the late Ming push toward monetizing a diverse tax base or revert back to earlier principles of collecting local tribute in kind? To what extent would local officials be allowed to negotiate tax relief for their jurisdictions? Would they encourage transregional and overseas trade? If so, where would such transactions be permitted to operate, and how much would the State extract from the profit? Just as in the cultural realm, it took some time for Qing fiscal policy to reconfigure the relationship of the State vis-à-vis its tax base. The issue of pharmaceutical objecthood is again indicative of the Qing approach to governance, as an abundant supply of materia medica remained essential for the sustenance of the State. The ways in which different branches of the Qing government acquired their remedies thus formed an important context for the continued development of the pharmaceutical trade and other business enterprises in the eighteenth century.
1648年，清军夺取北京、宣称受天命四年之后，一道敕令传到宁国府（见地图0.2），索取土贡药物黄连——一种味苦、多节的根，据说生长在宁国的名山中。经过对明末数十年积欠税赋的系统核查，确定应立即解送共计一千七百斤（逾一千公斤）的珍贵药材。
In 1648, four years after the Qing seized Beijing and claimed the Mandate of Heaven, an imperial decree arrived in the Ningguo Prefecture (see map 0.2) demanding the tribute medicine Golden Thread (
huanglian

), a bitter, knotty root known to grow in Ningguo’s famous mountains. Following a systematic review of the backlog in tax payment accumulated during the last decades of Ming rule, it was determined that a total of 1,700 jin (over 1,000 kilograms) of the precious medicine was to be dispatched immediately.
这道敕令在仍受战争创伤困扰的地方社会引发了一场小危机。府志记载，早在十一世纪，宋廷每年从宁国征收二十斤黄连作为土贡。明代的定额数量虽高得多，却早已折银缴纳。地方士绅推断，清廷当局突然索取，很可能是由于近年叛乱与战乱导致四川黄连市场供应减少、价格飞涨。于是，北京各部中有人把宁国当作这种要紧药材的替代来源。

The decree stirred a small crisis in the local community, still reeling from the traumas of war. The prefectural gazetteer recorded that back in the eleventh century, the Song state collected twenty jin of Golden Thread as tribute from Ningguo each year. The Ming quota, although much higher in quantity, had long been converted to payment in silver. The local gentry reasoned that the sudden request from the Qing administration was probably triggered by the diminished market supply of Golden Thread from Sichuan as a result of the recent rebellions and warfare, which had caused the price to soar. As a result, someone in the Beijing ministries had turned to Ningguo as an alternative source for the essential medicine.
为寻求解决办法，宁国知府与地方士绅合作，派人入山搜寻这种珍贵植物。省督很快得到消息：本地黄连已被“掘尽”，无货可供土贡。知府进一步说明，此前所有黄连其实都是从长江商埠芜湖买来的。
知府提出，以银两附加税支付这一千七百斤黄连，并争取宁国籍京官的支持。北京当局最终同意银、药兼收，并在八年内全部折银。

In search of a solution, the Ningguo prefect teamed up with local gentry and sent crews to search for the valuable plant in the mountains. The provincial governor shortly received word that native Golden Thread had been “completely dug out” and there was none to be had as tribute. The prefect offered further details by saying that all previous shipments of Golden Thread had in fact been purchased from Wuhu, a commercial hub on the Yangzi River.

The prefect offered to pay for the 1,700 jin of Golden Thread in silver cash as a surtax and gathered additional support from Ningguo natives among the capital civil officials. Authorities in Beijing eventually settled for a combination of silver and the medicine itself to be fully monetized in eight years’ time.

此案表明，中央与地方行政之间熟悉的讨价还价模式，如何跨越朝代更替而延续。宁国精英动员地方知识（黄连并不存在）来抵制中央对土贡物品的索取，这一套路我们已在第二章见过。如此，他们也间接揭示了跨区域药材贸易的情形：芜湖位于江西北端，那里出售的药材，许多应来自赣江上游的樟树等市镇（地图0.2）。方以智1660年代在樟树所见的地方变种，正与宁国知府关于同一药材川产与淮产（宁国被视为淮产范围）差异的论证相互印证。最终，北京各部与地方角色都把市场视为价值的最终仲裁者。

This case shows how the familiar pattern of bargaining between central and local administrations continued across dynastic transition. The elite of Ningguo mobilized local knowledge (the nonexistence of Golden Thread) to resist centralized demand for tribute items, a trope that we have seen in chapter 2. In so doing, they offered oblique insight into the interregional pharmaceutical trade, for Wuhu was situated at the northern tip of Jiangxi, and much of the materia medica on sale there would have been supplied from market towns upstream of the Gan River such as Zhangshu (map 0.2). The regional varieties that Fang Yizhi saw in Zhangshu in the 1660s were corroborated by the Ningguo prefect’s argument about the differences between the Sichuan and the Huai (of which Ningguo was considered a part) varieties of the same herb. In the end, both the Beijing ministries and the local players looked to the marketplace as the final arbiter of value.

史家指出，晚明所谓一条鞭法改革，意在把各种形式的税赋折银，却直到清朝统治下才在所有省份全面实施。
货币成为清代国家抽取、分配剩余财富的核心工具与主要会计单位。在此过程中，治理的性质与国家对土地特定物产的直接索取相脱离，转而取决于劳动力与自然资源的商品化。如果市场能够供应四川黄连，国家便愿意用从宁国征得的收入去买。

Historians have pointed out that the so-called Single Whip Law reforms of the late Ming, intended to convert diverse forms of taxation into silver, only came to be fully implemented in all provinces under Qing rule.

Money became the central instrument and chief unit of accounting for the Qing state to use to extract and allocate surplus wealth. In the process, the nature of governance came to be disassociated from the state’s direct claim to the specific products of the land, hinging instead on the commodification of labor and natural resources. If the marketplace was able to supply Golden Thread from Sichuan, the State was willing to buy it with revenue gathered from Ningguo.
1663年，清廷下令，一切田赋、徭役与地方土贡都直接解送北京户部。药材、牲畜与历日纸不再由地方官府大批运往礼部。改为由太医院直接为药房采购药材，再由户部报销。
由此，内廷与外朝的交易被置于更严密的簿记与定期审核之下，清政府的各个衙门成为商业供应商的直接顾客。偶尔，省级官员仍会采办实物贡品进呈皇帝。然而值得注意的是，药材大体上退出了常规土贡清单，让位于各地名茶、瓷器及其他制造品。反过来，十八世纪的清朝皇帝频繁下令制作“锭子药”，作为礼物赐给官员。
医药赠予的方向，已由自下而上逆转为自上而下。

In 1663, the Qing court ordered that all agricultural taxes, labor levees, and local tributes be paid directly to the Ministry of Revenue in Beijing. Medicines, livestock, and calendar papers would no longer be shipped in bulk from local administrations to the Ministry of Rites. Instead, the Imperial Academy of Medicine directly purchased ingredients for their pharmacy and got reimbursement from the Ministry of Revenue.

In this way, transactions between the inner and outer court came under the closer scrutiny of bookkeeping and periodic reviews, and the various offices of the Qing government became direct customers of mercantile suppliers. Occasionally, provincial administrators still procured tribute items in kind and sent them to the emperor. Yet remarkably materia medica were largely taken out from regular tribute lists, giving way instead to regional varieties of fine tea, porcelain, and other manufactured goods. Conversely, Qing emperors in the eighteenth century frequently ordered the manufacturing of “ingot medicine” (
dingzi yao
) to be given out as gifts to officials.
The directionality of medical gift-giving had been reversed from bottom-up to top-down.
十八世纪后期，皇帝内廷人员与外朝各部之间熟悉的紧张，再次集中体现于药物的分配。内务府——由满洲统治者亲信包衣（booi）管理的一个庞大机构——掌管一切内廷事务，并经营一个独立的御药房（yuyaofang），其权力逐渐盖过太医院。
内务府的专属收入来源，包括其广袤田产所收地租，以及常关、海关抽取的过境税。
十八世纪初的记载表明，清廷定期监控主要城市市场与宁波这样的海上贸易枢纽附近二三百种常用药材的贸易；往返日本长崎的船只载运大量中国原产或由中国商人经手的药材（这些侨居商人正是中川在日本采访、了解清代中国日常生活的人）。来自四川的最贵重道地药材，须缴纳与其它奢侈品相当的高税。
直到十九世纪，药材仍是区域与全球贸易的重要组成部分；中国始终是药材原料的主要出口国，同时也从日本、朝鲜、东南亚进口新品种，还有著名的美洲人参。我们将在第六章考察这一贸易对药学知识的影响。

Later in the eighteenth century, the familiar tension between the emperor’s inner court personnel and the outer court ministries was epitomized again in the allocation of medicine. The Imperial Household Department (
Neiwufu
), a sprawling organization run by the Manchu rulers’ trusted bondservants (Ma.
booi
), was in charge of all inner court affairs and ran a separate Imperial Pharmacy (
yuyaofang
) that came to eclipse the authority of the Imperial Academy of Medicine.
The Imperial Household Department’s exclusive source of income included rent collected from its vast tracts of land and transit tax extracted by domestic and maritime customs houses.

Early eighteenth-century records indicate that the Qing state regularly monitored the trade of 200–300 common kinds of materia medica near major urban markets and maritime trade hubs such as the port city of Ningbo, where ships to and from Japan’s Nagasaki carried large quantities of medicine native to China or brokered by Chinese merchants (these sojourning merchants were the ones interviewed by Nakagawa in Japan about everyday life in Qing China). The most valuable daodi medicine from Sichuan was subject to a higher duty on par with other luxury items.

Medicine continued to be a significant component of regional and global trade well into the nineteenth century, as China remained a major exporter of pharmaceutical ingredients and also imported new varieties from Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia, and, famously, ginseng from America. We will examine the impact this trade had on pharmaceutical knowledge in chapter 6.
与外朝各部不同，内务府并不满足于收支相抵，而是积极投资商贸以最大化利润。整个十八世纪，内务府向私营生意放高利贷，称之为“生息银两”（shengxi yinliang）。另一项有利可图的活动，是发放满洲故土所产人参的专卖许可；此时国家权力已严禁外人采挖。据史家 蒋竹山 的研究，内务府对额外收入的无休止追求，在很大程度上导致乾隆朝晚期满洲人参的市场价格涨至天价。
从税基持续货币化开始，清政权推行重商主义政策，鼓励商品化地方物产的贸易，并从其独占的特定场所获取非常利润。在此过程中，皇帝的私人代理人指定商业伙伴合作，并培育他们在社会中的特权。由于内务府的事业几乎完全在常规文官体系之外进行，批评或外部审核的空间极小。当时，敢于对皇帝私财提出异议的文官并不多。

Unlike the outer court ministries, the Imperial Household Department was not merely content with making ends meet but aggressively invested in trade and commerce to maximize profit. Throughout the eighteenth century, the Department made high-interest loans to private businesses, calling it “silver that grows and proliferates” (
shengxi yinliang

). Another profitable activity was licensing the dealership of ginseng harvested from the Manchu homeland, now strictly prohibited by state power from outside exploitations. According to historian Chiang Chu-shan’s study, the Department’s relentless pursuit of additional income did much to cause the market price for Manchurian ginseng to rise to exorbitant levels in the late years of the Qianlong reign.

Starting with the continued monetization of the tax base, the Qing regime pursued a mercantilist policy to encourage trade in commoditized local products, reaping extraordinary profits from selected venues to which it laid exclusive claim. In so doing, the emperor’s personal agents worked with designated business partners and nurtured their privilege in society. Since the ventures of the Imperial Household Department took place almost entirely outside of regular civil bureaucracy, there was little room for criticism or external review. At this time, not many of the civil officials would have dared to raise objection to the emperor’s private wealth.
在某种意义上，常规国家财政实践与内廷不受约束的投资之间的分隔，映照了公共文化中的知识重分类：医学正统在修辞上类似于儒学正统，却不必与之完全可通约。如果统一性与道德真理权威的最终根据只掌握在君主手中，那么他的个人行为——包括沉溺于追逐财富与权力——也依然不受常规官僚监督。在重商主义逻辑与专制统治共生的时代，晚明官员对君主滥用权力的批评变得沉寂了。

In a way, the partitioning of regular state fiscal practices from the unregulated investments of the inner court mirrored the reclassification of knowledge in public culture: that the orthodoxy of medicine resembled in rhetoric, but did not need to be entirely commensurable with, the orthodoxy of Confucian learning. If the ultimate ground for unity and authority over moral truth resided in the hands of the monarch alone, then his personal actions, including indulgence in the pursuit of wealth and power, would also remain immune to regular bureaucratic oversight. The late Ming officials’ critique of the ruler’s abuse of his power became muted in an age of mercantilist logic, symbiotic to autocratic rule.
在因与国家做生意而获益的商业角色中，为清廷独家供应药材的人，最终成为非常成功的企业家；他们夸耀自己的宫廷关系，以在市场上取得竞争优势。
我们接下来要考察的北京同仁堂，就是这样的例子。

Among the mercantile actors who benefited from business liaisons with the State, the exclusive purveyors of materia medica for the Qing court eventually became highly successful entrepreneurs who boasted their imperial connections to earn a competitive edge in the marketplace.
Such was the case of the Beijing pharmacy Tongrentang that we will examine next.

The Pharmacist’s Progress
1736年，清宫五位画家合作，仿《清明上河图》风格创作了一幅新长卷。画中城市景观在布局上类似十二世纪原作与晚明《苏州片》：蜿蜒的河流、桥下穿行的船只、雄伟城墙与熙攘街景。然而许多细节颇不相同。

例如，在这幅长11.5米的长卷中，清代宫廷画家把城市药铺画在比医者店铺显眼得多的位置，后者几乎不引人注意。一位儿科医者站在侧街，向登门的病人躬身施礼，店铺只有一块招牌：“贫不计利”。另一处清静的房舍是“祝由科”的居所。相形之下，两家药铺显得生气勃勃、颇具吸引力：学徒忙于切药，把一盘盘药材搬上屋顶晾晒，称量送到店门口的包裹（图5.2）。两家店铺都挂有多块招牌，宣传“川广道地药材”。药材的绚丽描绘，配以成包的货运，显示店主的商业网络。十八世纪后期，为1759年乾隆南巡而作的另一幅城市景观长卷《姑苏繁华图》，也画了多家出售“川广云贵”货物的药铺，却不见一间医者诊所。
总体而言，盛清城市景观画表明，人们期待药师在城市生活中扮演比个体医者活跃得多的角色。
In 1736, five artists at the Qing court collaborated to create a new scroll painting after the style of
Along the River during the Qingming Festival

. The urban landscape depicted resembled the twelfth-century original and late Ming Suzhou Scrolls in its organization: a meandering river, a boat passing beneath a bridge, a magnificent city wall and bustling street scenes. Yet many details were quite different.

For example, in the 11.5-meters-long scroll, the Qing palace painters depicted urban pharmacies at much more prominent locations than the shops of physicians, which became almost inconspicuous. A pediatrician stands on a side street, bowing to his visiting patients, his shop only featuring one sign, “the poor are treated without concern for profit” (
pin bu ji li
). Another quiet building was the residence of an “incantation exorcism specialist” (
zhuyou ke

). Two pharmacy shops, by contrast, appear much more dynamic and appealing: apprentices are busy cutting herbs, carrying trays of materia medica up to the roof for drying, and weighing packages delivered to the shop’s front door (figure 5.2). Both shops feature multiple signs, advertising “authentic (
daodi
) medicine from Chuan-Guang.” The colorful depiction of materia medica is coupled with packaged shipments that indicate the business connections of the shop owners. Later in the eighteenth century,
Prosperous Suzhou

, another scroll painting of urban landscape commissioned for the occasion of the Qianlong emperor’s southern tour in 1759, also depicted various pharmacies featuring merchandise from “Chuan-Guang-Yun(nan)-Gui(zhou)” but not a single physician’s office.
Overall, High Qing urban landscape paintings indicated that pharmacists were expected to play a much more active role in city life than individual physicians.
这些画作印证了徐大椿的抱怨：医者无法对制药过程施加任何实际控制。开方医者与配药药师的分离，取代了早先医者作为药室主人的复合形象。正当本草被化为最易获取的文本形式时，医者却失去了对曾经引以为傲的制药技艺的掌控。

The paintings confirm Xu Dachun’s complaint about the inability of physicians to exert any real control over pharmaceutical processes. The separation between prescribing physicians and dispensing pharmacists replaced the earlier composite image of the medical expert as master of the pharmaceutical chamber. Just when bencao was rendered into its most accessible textual form, physicians lost control over the artisanal techniques that had once been the pride of their trade.

药师的流行形象源自医者，却又与医者明确区分。同仁堂（“同仁”意为共同的人道）于1702年（康熙四十一年）在北京大栅栏商业区的黄金地段开业。店主乐凤鸣起初沿用明代旧称，把生意称作“药室”。据乐凤鸣说，店中独特的产品来自他已故父亲乐尊育的医学训练；乐尊育曾在太医院任吏目（limu）。乐家世代为走方医，老乐以善于辨识道地药材的细微差别闻名，他配制的成药广受欢迎、疗效显著。尽管同仁堂自称源于某位医者的技艺，却逐渐被一致称作“药铺”。乐凤鸣的后人不再行医，而自视为“知药而不知医”（zhi yao bu zhi yi）。1700年代中期，乐家把同仁堂卖给另一位同样不行医的店主。

The popular image of the pharmacist was derived from that of the physician but also explicitly distinguished from it. The pharmacy shop Tongrentang (Hall of Common Humanity) opened for business in 1702 (Kangxi 41), at a prime location in the Dashilan commercial district of Beijing. At first, the owner, Yue Fengming, referred to the business as a pharmaceutical chamber (
yaoshi
) after the Ming fashion. In Yue’s account, the shop’s unique products came from the medical training of his late father, Yue Zunyu, who had served as a clerk (
limu
) in the Imperial Academy of Medicine. Having descended from a lineage of itinerant healers, the senior Yue was well known for his ability to “tell the subtle features of authentic [
didao] materia medica

,” and the compound medicines he made were popular and efficacious. Despite its alleged origin in the skill of an individual physician, Tongrentang came to be consistently referred to as a pharmacy shop (
yaopu
). Descendants of Yue Fengming no longer practiced medicine but saw themselves as “knowing the remedies but not [the art of] medicine” (
zhi yao bu zhi yi
). In the mid-1700s, the Yue family sold Tongrentang to another owner who also did not practice medicine.

如果药师未必是疗愈者，他又如何向顾客担保所售药物的疗效？同仁堂的店主首先诉诸古方（gufang）永恒的功效。在1706年为同仁堂第一部药目所写的序中，乐凤鸣坚称：若药不能治病，问题必定出在药材质量或配制过程。于是，乐凤鸣提出了药铺的承诺，后来成为店训：

If the pharmacist was not necessarily a healer, then how could he vouch for the efficacy of what he sold to the customers? Tongrentang’s owners started off by asserting the timeless efficacy of ancient recipes (
gufang

). In his 1706 preface to Tongrentang’s first catalog, Yue Fengming insisted that if a drug failed to cure, the problem must have been either the quality of ingredients or the process of compounding. Hence Yue laid out the pharmacy’s promise that would become the shop’s guiding mantra:

“遵肘后，辨地产；
炮制虽繁必不敢省人工，
品味虽贵必不敢减物力。
可以质鬼神，可以应病症。”

Follow the
Recipes at Hand

, and distinguish the products’ places of origin;
Complex as the pharmaceutical procedures are, we never spare our labor.
Costly as the ingredients are, we never compromise on the material expenses.
Gods and ghosts will judge us, and our products will respond to all sorts of illnesses.

对物料本真性与技术本真性的双重强调，与对著名“古方”的依赖相得益彰。药师虽不声称懂医，却誓言把方剂化为有效良药。从文本到商品的顺畅转化，一方面由获得道地药材保证，另一方面由一丝不苟的炮制执行保证。在这两方面，药铺都比个体医者更具竞争优势；后者平均而言资本较少，难以从批发市场购买药材或雇工。

The dual emphasis on material and technical authenticity dovetailed nicely with the dependence on well-known, “ancient” recipes. Although the pharmacist did not profess to know medicine, he vowed to render recipes into potent cures. The smooth translation from text to commodity was in turn guaranteed by access to daodi authentic ingredients on the one hand, and fastidious execution of pharmaceutical processes on the other. In doing both, pharmacies held a competitive edge over individual practitioners who, on average, possessed less capital to purchase ingredients from the wholesale marketplace or to hire labor.
除此之外，药师还以无可置疑的虔诚换取顾客信任。正如同仁堂另一句店训所言：“修合无人见，存心有天知。”城市药师竞相以道德虔诚的最佳典范出现。与清廷重商主义政策遵循类似逻辑，十八世纪的精英药师力图让顾客相信：药物的疗效与其市场价值是一致的。个体生命之康健，正如政体之康健，都可以用金钱来复兴。
编者说明：同仁堂现行店训作“修合无人见，存心有天知”；其作为店训的最早出现年代仍待历史文献核实。

In addition to that, the pharmacist also asked for customers’ trust by pledging undisputable piety. As another business slogan of Tongrentang asserted, “no one sees how we compound / yet Heaven alone knows our mind.” Urban pharmacists competed to appear as the best exemplar of moral piety. Taking up a similar logic to the Qing state’s mercantilist policies, elite pharmacists of the eighteenth century sought to convince their customers that the efficacy of medical remedies was congruent to their market value. The wellbeing of individual lives, just like that of the polity, could be rejuvenated with money.
Editor's note (Chinese): 同仁堂现行店训作“修合无人见，存心有天知”；其作为店训的最早出现年代仍待历史文献核实。
撇开宏大修辞，清代药师所刊现存的少数几部药目中，透露出他们在激烈竞争中的挣扎。从个体医者拥有的药室，转变为雇用十五至二十名帮手的药铺，并非易事。
鹤年堂是十八世纪中叶北京另一家老字号药铺，直到1758年才刊行药目，据英文底本转述，此时已悉心经营数十年。鹤年堂距同仁堂仅两公里，毗邻繁忙的菜市口，也自称曾为清宫供应药材，并与京官保持密切关系；药目中收有五名中高级官员所写的多篇序文，可见一斑。
据英文底本转述，店主也承认自己未精通家传医术，但誓言确保药材道地、炮制合宜。或许是为回应鹤年堂的挑战，同仁堂也在1764年重刊了自己的药目新版。
两家药铺都提供种类繁多的成药——同仁堂1764年药目载有352种成药，治疗从头到脚的各种病症——但都没有在药目中披露实际配方。尽管有虔诚与仁义的修辞，这类出版物的意图仍是把顾客引进自家店门，而不是竞争对手的店门。

Grandiose rhetoric aside, the few extant catalogs published by Qing pharmacists hinted at their struggles amid fierce competition. The transition from individual, physician-owned pharmaceutical chambers to pharmacy shops that employed up to 15–20 hired hands was not easy.

Heniantang (Hall of Crane-like Longevity), another established pharmacy in mid-eighteenth- century Beijing, only issued a printed catalog in 1758, after “a few decades of careful practice.” Located only two kilometers from Tongrentang and adjacent to the busy vegetable market intersection (
Caishikou

), Heniantang also claimed access to the Qing imperial court as a purveyor of materia medica and nurtured close ties with capital officials, as seen from the multiple prefaces written by five mid- to high-level bureaucrats in the catalog.
The owner also confessed that he “had not mastered my family’s art of medicine” but pledged to “insure the authenticity of our
materia medica
, and the appropriateness of pharmaceutical procedures.” Perhaps in response to Heniantang’s challenge, Tongrentang also reissued a new edition of its own catalog in 1764.

Both pharmacies offered a wide range of compound drugs—the 1764 catalog of Tongrentang described 352 compound drugs treating all complaints from head to toe—but did not disclose the actual formulas in the catalog. The rhetoric of piety and humanity (
ren
) notwithstanding, the intention of such publications was still to get customers into their store rather than that of a competitor.

与那些结交宫廷代理人的精英药铺相比，别处崭露头角的药师另寻成功之道。1790年，一家名为敬修堂的新药铺在广州开业；广州是朝廷指定对欧洲商人开放的口岸。药铺创办人钱树田原是绸缎商，来自宁波港附近的慈溪县，当地以药材商世家闻名（见地图0.2）。据说钱树田在广州逗留期间治好了一位富家子弟。病家邀他留下，并出资帮他开店。
1804年，钱树田决定刊行一部药目以推广品牌，题为《敬修堂药说》。

Compared to elite shops with connections to imperial agents, up-and-coming pharmacists elsewhere found other strategies to achieve business success. In 1790, a new pharmacy named Jingxiutang (Hall of Respectful Cultivation) opened for business in the city of Canton, the designated port for trade with European merchants. The pharmacy was founded by Qian Shutian, a silk dealer who hailed from Cixi County, a town near the port of Ningbo known for its lineages of pharmaceutical merchants (see map 0.2). During his sojourn in Canton, Qian reportedly cured the son of a wealthy man. The patient’s family invited him to stay and provided him with funds to open his own shop.
In 1804, Qian Shutian decided to promote his brand by issuing a printed catalog, which he titled
Jingxiutang yao shuo (Discourses on the Drugs of Jingxiutang
总体而言，这部药目无法与同仁堂、鹤年堂的宏富品种相比。钱氏药铺只能生产七十种成药，但他把自己最畅销的几种“经验”良方加以定制，并大力宣传。另一大不同，是钱树田为每种成药标价，表明他指望药目直接带来顾客订单。在序中，钱氏搬用熟悉的说辞：使用道地药材，并以精细费工的工序炮制。钱氏尤其夸耀自己的特效药灵验无比，据英文底本译述，可比能够随心调用的精金。
对敬修堂这样规模较小、成立较晚的企业而言，药师往往先靠几种有效的秘方立足——堪比十九世纪世界流行的“专利药”——再逐渐获得配制更多常规成药的能力。

Overall, the catalog was no match for the impressive repertoire of Tongrentang and Heniantang. Qian’s pharmacy could only produce up to seventy compound drugs, yet he customized a few of his best-selling “tried and true” (
jingyan

) remedies and advertised them aggressively. Another major difference was that Qian Shutian listed the price for each compound drug, suggesting that he expected the catalog to directly bring in new orders from customers. In his preface, Qian mobilized the familiar rhetoric of using authentic (
daodi

) ingredients and labor-intensive pharmaceutical procedures that were “expertly handled to perfection.” In particular, Qian boasted that his special cures were so efficacious that they could be compared with “refined gold, deployable as one wishes.”

For smaller and newer enterprises like Jingxiutang, pharmacists often sought to establish themselves with a few effective secret remedies—comparable to the “patent drugs” popular in the nineteenth-century world—and gradually acquired the capacity to concoct a wider range of regular compound medicines.

钱树田的创业生涯起于无关商品的跨区域贸易，未必出自医学背景。清宫藏书中发现了一部敬修堂药目，说明钱氏的药物成功引起了御药房药师的注意。尽管地域出身各异，清代药师通过接入一体化的国内市场而找到共同点。帝国各地的新药铺相互仿效，模仿彼此的产品，使用同一套本真、虔诚与灵巧的语言。

Qian Shutian’s entrepreneurial career took off from the interregional trade of unrelated merchandise, not necessarily from a medical background. A copy of Jingxiutang’s catalog was discovered in the Qing imperial collection, indicating that Qian’s remedies successfully gained the attention of the imperial pharmacists. Despite their distinct regional origins, Qing pharmacists found common ground via their connections to an integrated domestic marketplace. All over the empire, new shops modeled themselves after each other, imitating each other’s products and evoking the same language of authenticity, piety, and ingenuity.

在本章中，我勾勒了市场与城市药铺在中国早期近代医疗图景中不断变化的角色。开方而不施药的医者，与连接全国市场、制造成药的药师之间的分工，到十八世纪末已成为清代城市生活的重要标志。批发商、牙人、店主及其学徒的群体，取代了早先医学家庭的小规模经营。用梁其姿（Angela Ki-Che Leung）的话说，十六世纪前后国家指定医疗机构的消失，标志着“有组织医学”衰落的开端。我们在清代中国看到一种新的有组织疗愈模式，它依靠药学的商品化，却不受国家监管。

In this chapter, I have sketched out the changing roles of the marketplace and the urban pharmacies in China’s early modern medical scene. The division of labor between physicians, who prescribed without dispensing medicine, and pharmacists, who were connected to a national market and manufactured compound cures, became an important indicator of urban living in Qing China by the end of the eighteenth century. The communities of wholesale dealers, brokers, shop owners, and their apprentices replaced the small-scale operation of medical households in earlier times. In Angela Ki-Che Leung’s words, the disappearance of the state-designated medical institutions around the sixteenth century marked the beginning of the decline of “organized medicine.” We see in Qing China a
new
organized model of healing that hinged on the commodification of pharmacy without state supervision.

这种在清代城市景观画中——后来又在外国访客的文学与摄影游记中——显著呈现的新“有组织医学”，其凝聚力并非来自中央设计的制度与标准化考试，而是来自对一体化国内市场的接入。然而，理解这一现象的困难在于：这一贸易的大多数参与者不断流动，基本处于官方视野之外。他们给家乡与新居地的社会经济结构带来的巨变，只能通过间接证据与后代的追溯记载来体察。例如，地方官须对影响行商安全的盗匪或抢劫案件负责；清廷档案中的大量报告因此记录了受害者的姓名、损失程度与行程。
比起远赴他乡的本地男儿，樟树地方志更纪念了数十位烈女（lienü），她们的丈夫在湖南、广西、云南等西南省份经商时去世。
有一则事例：一名年轻女子从广西一路来到樟树镇，自称嫁给的商人现已去世。故事结局圆满：这位丧夫的陌生女子被丈夫的大家族接纳，在此度过余生。

This new “organized medicine” that was featured prominently in Qing urban landscape paintings—and later, in the literary and photographic travelogues of foreign visitors—derived its coherence not from centrally designed institutions and standardized examinations, but rather from access to an integrated domestic market. The challenge of understanding this phenomenon, however, lies in the fact that most participants to this trade were constantly on the move and stayed largely outside official purview. The sea change they brought to the socioeconomic fabric of both their native places and their new homes can only be fathomed through indirect evidence and retrospective accounts from later generations. For instance, local officials were held responsible for banditry or robbery cases that affected the security of traveling mer- chants; numerous reports in the Qing state archive therefore recorded the victims’ names, extent of loss, and itineraries.
More so than the native sons who migrated to faraway places, the local gazetteer of Zhangshu commemorated dozens of virtuous women (
lienü
) whose husbands died while doing business in southwestern provinces such as Hunan, Guangxi, and Yunnan.

In one incident, a young woman traveled all the way from Guangxi to the town of Zhangshu and introduced herself as having married a merchant who had now died. The story had a happy ending as the bereaved stranger was accepted by her husband’s extended family and lived the rest of her life there.

另一方面，现代关于清代商业组织的记述，为弥补官方记载的缺失而矫枉过正，几乎把起源故事奉为神圣。同仁堂便是一例：药铺的官方历史受制于从原店发展而来的现代公司的利益。公司的长寿被引为乐家德行与经营才能的证明；乐平泉（1810—1880）及其妻许叶芬（1827—1907）等成功人物，如今已成为流行文化中的名人，包括以乐家故事为蓝本的电视剧。随着中医在二十世纪获得民族主义的光环，同仁堂自称坚持制作“古方”，也获得了额外的政治吸引力。
同样，樟树那些著名药帮（yaobang）的历史，被写得仿佛此镇自古以来便注定要大获成功。
这批文献的丰富潜力，尚待仔细发掘其中能说明问题的细节，例如店主、账房、库房与学徒各自在自己的群体中交往的独立行会。
我们还从口述史中得知，二十世纪初，年轻的药铺学徒每月可领剃头三次的津贴，另有顾客给的小费，通常还获准与同伙喝茶、吸烟。行内人人都要学会背诵十七世纪作者流行的两部药学入门书。

Modern accounts of Qing business organization, on the other hand, overcorrected the lack of official records by granting the origin stories almost sacrosanct status. Tongrentang is a case in point, as the official history of the pharmacy was beholden to the interests of the modern-day company that descended from the original shop. The longevity of the company has been cited as proof of the Yue family’s virtue and business prowess, and successful figures such as Yue Pingquan (1810–80) and his wife Xu Yefen (1827–1907) have become celebrated figures in popular culture today, including TV dramas based on the Yue family’s stories. As TCM acquired a nationalistic aura over the twentieth century, Tongrentang’s professed commitment to manufacturing “ancient recipes” gained extra political appeal.
Similarly, the celebrated pharmaceutical companies (
yaobang
) of Zhangshu were documented as if the town had been destined for great success since time immemorial.

The rich potential of this literature has yet to be carefully mined for telling details, such as the existence of separate guilds where shop owners, accountants, storage keepers, and apprentices socialized within their own groups.

We also learn from oral histories that in early twentieth century a young pharmacy apprentice would receive a stipend to shave his head three times a month, in addition to tips from customers, and was typically allowed to drink tea and smoke with his coworkers. Everybody in the trade learned to recite two primer pharmacy texts popularized by seventeenth-century authors.
